title: Remember Me — Dreams, Interpretations, Forgetting
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Let me start today with a very everyday question: which is harder to bear — being turned down, or being forgotten?

Being turned down at least leaves you with an answer. Being forgotten does not even leave you that much — you wait, and you have no idea how long you are waiting for, and you are not even sure the other person still remembers that there was anything to remember.

In Genesis 40, Joseph is in prison. Out of sheer kindness he takes an interest in two fellow prisoners, he interprets their dreams exactly, and then he asks one thing of them, very politely: "But remember me when it is well with you."
The last verse of this chapter reads, "Yet the chief cup bearer didn't remember Joseph, but forgot him." And then the first words of chapter 41 are, "At the end of two full years."
1. Why Do You Look So Sad Today?

"After these things, the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker offended their lord, the king of Egypt. Pharaoh was angry … He put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, into the prison, the place where Joseph was bound." (Genesis 40:1–3)
The narrator goes out of his way to add one clause: "the place where Joseph was bound." He wants us to know that this is not a coincidence.

"Cup bearer" in the original is מַשְׁקֵה (*mashqeh*) — the man who poured the king's wine and also tasted it for him against poison, the closest and most trusted post in the whole court. The "chief baker" was the steward over the king's table. These two are not ordinary prisoners. They are senior officers of the palace.
Verse 4: "The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he took care of them."

"Took care of" is וַיְשָׁרֶת (*vayesharet*) in the original, and it is the same word as in the chapter before, where Joseph "ministered to" his master. Later, in the books of the law, this very word becomes the technical term for a priest ministering in the sanctuary.
Brothers and sisters, here is a man locked up on a charge he never earned, and inside that prison he ministers to two new arrivals. That fact by itself is a sermon.

And then comes the verse in this chapter that impresses me most: "Joseph came in to them in the morning, and saw them, and saw that they were sad. He asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, saying, 'Why do you look so sad today?'" (Genesis 40:6–7)
"Sad" in the original is זֹעֲפִים (*zo'aphim*) — it means their faces had gone dark.

Think for a moment about where Joseph himself is standing. Sold by his own brothers. Falsely accused. Shut away for years. Not one person has spoken a single word on his behalf. He has a hundred good reasons to keep his head down all day long.
But when he came in that morning, he saw somebody else's face.

Brothers and sisters, when a person is in pain, the most natural reaction in the world is to stop seeing other people. The eyes pull inward, and the whole world shrinks down to the one thing that is happening to you. Joseph did not do that. In the middle of his own hard season he still noticed that somebody else was not himself today.
That is a form of spiritual health. You can use this one verse to take your own temperature: this week, have I looked into anybody's face — anybody's at all — and actually seen it?
They said, "We have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it." Every dream interpreter in Egypt was up at the palace; these two were down in the prison.
Joseph's answer is the theological heart of the whole chapter: "Don't interpretations belong to God? Please tell it to me." (Genesis 40:8)
The Hebrew is הֲלוֹא לֵאלֹהִים פִּתְרֹנִים (*halo lElohim pitronim*), literally "do not interpretations belong to God?"

Do you feel how costly that sentence is? At this moment the one piece of leverage he still has in his hand is that gift. He could very easily have said, "I can interpret dreams," and raised his own price a little. Instead, with his very first sentence, he pushes the credit away from himself.

A man who is in the habit of giving God the glory in the small places will not forget to do it standing in front of a king. In chapter 41, when he is standing before Pharaoh, his first sentence is still this: "It isn't in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace."
Habits are formed in the places where nobody is watching.
Joseph was in prison himself. How was he still able to see the look on somebody else's face?

Verse 6 says, "Joseph came in to them in the morning, and saw them, and saw that they were sad," and then he opens his mouth and asks, "Why do you look so sad today?" Think about where he is standing. Sold by his own brothers. Falsely accused. Shut away for years. Not one person speaking a word on his behalf. When a person is in pain, the most natural reaction there is is to stop seeing other people — the eyes pull inward, and the whole world shrinks down to the one thing that has happened to you. Joseph did not do that. That is a form of spiritual health, and it also makes a very good thermometer: this week, have I truly seen the look on anybody's face?
"Don't interpretations belong to God?" — why is that sentence so particularly hard to get out?

Because it was the only piece of leverage he had. He could have said, "I can interpret dreams," and raised his own price a little; a prisoner who wants to climb back up survives by making people remember what he is good at. Instead his very first sentence pushes the credit away. And you can see what that habit produced one chapter later: standing in front of Pharaoh, his first sentence is still "It isn't in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." Habits are formed where nobody is watching. So the thing to practise is not how you will give God the glory on some large occasion. It is what the first sentence out of your mouth will be today, in a small group, when somebody pays you a compliment.
2. A Light from the Original: Two Liftings of the Head

The cup bearer speaks first. He dreamed of a vine with three branches on it; it budded, it blossomed, and its clusters produced ripe grapes; and he pressed the grapes into Pharaoh's cup and put the cup into Pharaoh's hand.
Joseph says, "The three branches are three days … Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head, and restore you to your office."

That phrase is remarkable in the original: יִשָּׂא פַרְעֹה אֶת־רֹאשֶׁךָ (*yissa Pharaoh et-roshecha*), literally "Pharaoh will lift up your head." It is an idiom shared by Egyptian and Hebrew alike, and it means to set a man back in his place and give him his dignity again.

Then the chief baker, seeing that the interpretation had come out well, told his dream too. He dreamed that he was carrying three baskets of white bread on his head, and that in the uppermost basket was food for Pharaoh, and birds came down and ate it.
Joseph's interpretation opens with exactly the same words, not one of them altered:

"This is its interpretation. The three baskets are three days. Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head from off you, and will hang you on a tree; and the birds will eat your flesh from off you." (Genesis 40:18–19)
The original here also reads "Pharaoh will lift up your head" — only with three more words tacked onto the end: מֵעָלֶיךָ (*me'aleicha*), "from off you."

One and the same idiom. For one man it means his head is lifted and he goes back to his post; for the other it means his head is lifted — and taken off his body. The whole distance between them is three words.
Brothers and sisters, there is a lesson here we have to learn: Joseph did not change his answer.

He knew perfectly well how ugly that answer was going to sound. He could easily have blurred it a little — "I can't quite make your dream out" — and in three days the thing would have declared itself anyway, so why be the man who carries bad news?
But he said what God had given him to say. A man who carries God's word does not get to carry only the part of it he happens to be willing to say.
And notice that expression, "hang you on a tree." Deuteronomy 21 says, "he who is hanged is accursed of God." And Galatians quotes it: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."

This chapter has two men in it: one who lives because of a dream, and one who is hanged on a tree. And seventeen hundred years later, at Golgotha, there are two men again, one on the right hand and one on the left. And one of them says to the man in the middle, "Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom."
The same sentence. And this time the answer comes back: "Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise."
Joseph asked a man to remember him, and the man forgot him. The thief asked the Lord to remember him, and the Lord promised him on the spot.
It is the same idiom in both places. Why does it mean reinstatement for one man and beheading for the other?

"Pharaoh will lift up your head" is what the Hebrew says literally, and it is an idiom shared by Egyptian and Hebrew alike: to set a man back in his place and give him his dignity again. In the baker's paragraph the original uses that very same phrase — only with three more words on the end: "from off you." One and the same lifting of the head: for one man it means being lifted back into office, for the other it means having his head taken off his body. It is a chilling way to write, and it is also a reminder to read Scripture slowly: in Hebrew narrative the heaviest meaning is very often hidden in a difference of one or two words. And the real lesson of this passage lies in the next sentence — Joseph knew how ugly the answer was, and he still said it exactly as God had given it.
When you have bad news to give, is it all right to keep it a little vague?

Joseph could easily have said, "I can't quite make your dream out" — three days later it would all have come out by itself anyway, so why be the one who says it? But he said what God had given him. A man who carries God's word does not carry only the part he happens to be willing to say. Of course, this is not a licence to speak without mercy. In practice there are three principles. First, be sure that what you are saying really is what God said and not simply your own judgement. Second, let the way you say it take the other person's situation into account; if it can be said privately, do not say it publicly. Third, when you have said it, stay with him — do not drop one heavy sentence and walk away. Truth with company alongside it is pastoral care. Truth without company is merely being correct.
3. Remember Me — and He Forgot Him
When the interpreting was done, Joseph said the one and only sentence in this whole chapter that he says on his own behalf:

"But remember me when it is well with you. Please show kindness to me, and make mention of me to Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house. For indeed, I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon." (Genesis 40:14–15)
"Remember me" is זְכַרְתַּנִי (*zekartani*) in the original — the very same verb as in chapter 8, where "God remembered Noah."

And "show kindness to me" is חֶסֶד (*chesed*) — the previous chapter, at verse 21, says, "But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him," using exactly that word. What he is asking from a man is the very thing God has already shown him.
I want to stop here and say something that matters a great deal: Joseph opening his mouth to ask another person for help is not a failure of faith.

Somebody will say, "He should have looked to God alone; he had no business asking a man." Brothers and sisters, Paul asked the brothers and sisters again and again to pray for him, and he accepted the support the church at Philippi sent him. Asking for help is not unspiritual. Asking for help is honest.
If you are in need of help right now, please say so out loud. Do not grit your teeth and carry it alone because you think that asking would show too little faith.

And look at the way he states his own wrong: "For indeed, I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews." The Hebrew is גֻנֹּב גֻּנַּבְתִּי (*gunnov gunnavti*), the infinitive absolute, an emphatic construction — "stolen, I was truly stolen."

He states his wrong, and he names nobody. He does not say, "It was my brothers who sold me." He does not say, "It was Potiphar's wife who lied about me." He sets the facts out plainly, and he does not drag one single person out into the open.

And there is one more word. He says, "they should put me into the dungeon" — and the word the original uses there is בּוֹר (*bor*), a pit. It is the same word as that "pit" in chapter 37, the one his brothers threw him into.
The first pit of his life and the second pit of his life are written with the same word. Some people's lives really do run like that: you climb out of one pit and drop straight into the next.

Then in verses 20 to 22 everything comes about precisely as Joseph said it would. Pharaoh's birthday arrives and he sets out a feast — this is the first time the Bible ever mentions a birthday — the cup bearer is restored to his position, the baker is hanged, "as Joseph had interpreted to them."
The narrator sets his own seal on it: Joseph read it right, word for word.
And the last verse of the whole chapter is this:
"Yet the chief cup bearer didn't remember Joseph, but forgot him." (Genesis 40:23)

The original puts two near-synonyms back to back inside this one verse: "did not remember" (וְלֹא־זָכַר, *velo-zakar*) and "forgot him" (וַיִּשְׁכָּחֵהוּ, *vayyishkachehu*). Saying it once was not enough. It says it twice.
Brothers and sisters, that is how the chapter ends. No turn, no comfort, no "but Yahweh was with him." The chapter before had that "but." This one does not.
The text simply leaves us standing there.
Joseph opened his mouth and asked the cup bearer for help. Does that count as not trusting God?

It does not. The verb in "remember me" is the same word as in chapter 8, where "God remembered Noah," and the word behind "show kindness to me" is חֶסֶד — precisely the word the previous chapter uses when it says, "But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him." What he asks from a man is the very thing God has already shown him. And everything he says is true: he really had been stolen away, and he really had done nothing. So asking a person for help is not unbelief; go to the person you ought to go to, and make the appeal you ought to make. Only remember this: people may forget, and God will not. Put your hope in God and put your request into human ears — those two things can be done at the same time.
"Yet the chief cup bearer didn't remember Joseph, but forgot him" — why say the same thing twice over?

Hebrew commonly uses repetition to press the weight down: did not remember, and then forgot him. And straight after this verse, the first line of chapter 41 is "At the end of two full years." Scripture writes being forgotten this heavily because it really is that hard to bear — being turned down at least leaves you an answer, and being forgotten leaves you nothing at all to hold. But there is another side to see. If the cup bearer had remembered him there and then, Joseph might simply have been let out and sent back to the land of the Hebrews, and there would never have been that day of standing in front of Pharaoh. A human being's forgetting, seen inside God's timetable, is waiting; seen inside our own feelings, it is being dropped. Both of those are true at once.
And then the first words of chapter 41 are these: "At the end of two full years."
Two years. Seven hundred and thirty days. Every single morning he wakes up, and the cell is still the same cell.

I do not want to make those two years sound easy. They were two very hard years. He did every single thing right — he took a kind interest in other people, he delivered the message faithfully, he asked honestly for help — and what it earned him was two years of being forgotten.
But brothers and sisters, please read on with me into chapter 41:

Two years later, Pharaoh dreams. Every magician in Egypt is summoned and not one of them can interpret it. And at that moment the cup bearer suddenly remembers: "I remember my faults today." And he has Joseph brought up.
On that one day Joseph went straight from a prison cell to standing in front of the king — and before that same day was out he was the second man in Egypt.
Now think back with me for a moment: what if the cup bearer had remembered him that very day?

If he had spoken up for Joseph two years earlier, what is the best result you could hope for? A foreign slave is cleared and let out — and then what? He goes back to being the steward in Potiphar's house.
Out two years earlier, and what he gets is his freedom. Out two years later, and what he gets is the whole of Egypt.
Those two years were not a delay. They were an alignment. God was lining up the timing of two things: the release of one prisoner, and the dream of one king.

Let me say the next sentence very carefully. I am not saying that every season of waiting is exchanged in the end for a prime minister's seat. Scripture gives us no such guarantee, and I would not dare to give it either.
What I am saying is something else: God's timetable is reckoned by the kingdom, not reckoned by the length of our patience. And more than that —
The cup bearer forgot him. God did not forget.

Here is what being forgotten really means: that people do not remember me does not mean that I am not remembered. Isaiah 49 says, "Can a woman forget her nursing child … Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you! Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands."
A human being's remembering is written on the heart, and hearts forget. God's remembering is carved into his hands, and it leaves a scar.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
When this chapter is preached, there are several places where a preacher's hand slips very easily.

The first distortion is to say that Joseph should never have asked anybody for help, that he should have relied on God alone. Asking for help is not unbelief; Paul too asked again and again for prayer and accepted support. Preach it as unspiritual and the people in the room who genuinely need help will not dare to open their mouths. The test is this: when the person who needs help has heard you out, is he readier to ask — or lonelier than he was before?

The second distortion is to preach those "two years" as God punishing him, or as a test sent because his faith was not strong enough. The text gives no reason at all; what chapter 41 brings to light is an alignment of timing. Preach it as punishment and the people who are currently waiting will blame themselves twice as hard.

The third distortion is to present the interpreting of dreams as a technique you can learn or a gift you can be trained into. Joseph himself said, "Don't interpretations belong to God?" and later, "It isn't in me." Preach it as a technique and what the congregation goes chasing after is a power, not God.

The fourth distortion is to preach the cup bearer's ingratitude and never to preach God's remembering. The last line of the chapter stops at "forgot him" — but the answer the whole of Scripture gives is "yet I will not forget you." Stop at the ingratitude and all your congregation carries home is how cold the world is. The test is this: the last picture this sermon leaves behind — is it being forgotten, or being engraved?

The fifth distortion is to preach "prime minister two years later" as the rate of return on waiting. For some people the waiting never turns into a reversal on this side of the grave. Hebrews 11 is very honest about it: some received what was promised, and of others it says, "These all, having been commended for their faith, didn't receive the promise." The worth of a season of waiting does not lie in the size of the outcome. It lies in who it is that waits it out beside you.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question. We are very used to working through connections, and we are very easily wounded through connections. You ask somebody for a favour, and he says, "No problem at all, leave it with me" — and then there is no then. We are too embarrassed to chase it up, so it turns sour quietly inside us instead. Brothers and sisters, Joseph asked somebody for a favour, and that somebody forgot him. The text does not scold Joseph for asking, and it does not make excuses for the cup bearer either — it simply writes the thing down honestly. You may ask a person for help. Only do not stake your hope on a person's memory. Human memory breaks down; God's remembering does not. This week, if there is somebody in your heart who promised you something and never did it, cross that account out of the ledger you keep inside you and hand it over to God.

The second question. Our culture is deeply afraid of being the one who brings bad news. We dare not pass on what the doctor's report actually said. We dare not say out loud what is really going on at home. We see something wrong in the church and we walk around it — and we call that being gracious. But Joseph said the hardest sentence in the chapter to the baker's face. Brothers and sisters, real graciousness is not refusing to say it; real graciousness is saying it well. This week, if there is a sentence that is true and unpleasant to hear and it is yours to say to somebody, carry it with love and say it. Speaking the truth in love — you need both halves of that.
I have been forgotten. I have been passed over. How do I live through two years of that?

Begin by admitting that it really does hurt; do not use "God has a good purpose in it" to dam your own feelings back up. The Psalms are full of prayers that ask, "How long?" Then there are three very practical things you can do. First, live the days with something in them: Joseph was a man with work to do inside that prison — he served, he managed — and what finally set him on his feet was the shape his character took during exactly that stretch of time. Second, keep a record that can be checked: what you did and when you did it, not so that you can demand justice, but so that you can speak clearly when the opportunity comes. Third, find one person who knows your situation and meet with him regularly. Waiting with nobody beside you is the fastest way for waiting to turn into bitterness.
7. Living 321 Out — Give God the Glory in the Small Places
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson and tie it back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Joseph interpreted two dreams: one man lived, and one man was hanged on a tree. And at Golgotha there were two men as well, one on each side, and one of them said, "remember me." Joseph asked a man to remember him and the man forgot; the thief asked the Lord to remember him, and the Lord said, "Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise." My role model is this: that one really did remember him — and remembered him on the spot.

The Bible is my standard. A standard is not "say what the other person wants to hear." A standard is: say the word God gave you, exactly as he gave it. Feeling says, "If I put it like that I will give offence." The standard says, "Let your 'Yes' be 'Yes' and your 'No' be 'No.'" The unpleasant half has to be said as well — only it has to be said carrying love.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When Joseph saw the look on those men's faces inside that prison, that was not emotional intelligence; that is the sensitivity that comes naturally to a person who has God in his heart. To rely on our intellect and lean on ourselves is to be eaten up with worry — a brain in a tight place does nothing but count its own losses over and over again. To rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit is to have gladness — a person with God in his heart still has eyes that can see other people.

Let Jesus be King. "Don't interpretations belong to God?" — in a place where nobody could see him, he had already handed the glory over. Letting Jesus be King is something you begin practising in the small places. The way you speak in your small group, at home, in a room with only two or three people in it, decides how you will speak one day when you are standing on a large stage.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The one piece of leverage Joseph had left in his hand was that gift, and with his first sentence he handed it back to God. The moment when we are most likely to keep the glory for ourselves is precisely the moment when we have only one thing left in our hands.

Establish God's system. God used those two years to line up the time of one prisoner with the dream of one king. His timetable is reckoned by the kingdom. To establish God's system you have to learn to look at things on God's clock — not asking, "Why has it still not happened?" but asking, "What are you lining this up with?"
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Season of Waiting
We walk through a season of waiting carrying one of four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "I do not need to ask anybody." Joseph asked. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights; it feels that opening your mouth to ask for help lowers your price. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and admitting that I need people and I need God. Asking for help will not make you smaller. Gritting your teeth alone is what makes you hard.

The fearful heart says, "What if this time comes to nothing as well?" It may very well come to nothing. Joseph's request came to nothing that time, and it went on coming to nothing for two years. But brothers and sisters, what you are afraid of is not that it will come to nothing. What you are afraid of is that nobody will remember you. The answer to this chapter is not to be found with the cup bearer. It is with the one who has engraved you on the palms of his hands.

The ashamed heart says, "I suppose I am simply not worth remembering." Being forgotten makes that reading come very easily. But Joseph's being forgotten had nothing whatever to do with his worth — he read those dreams right, word for word, and the narrator went out of his way to set his seal on it. When people forget you, it is usually because people are busy, not because you weigh so little.

The wounded heart says, "So all those years went for nothing." I will not tell you that those days did not hurt. What I will tell you is this: the first line of chapter 41 is "At the end of two full years," and then, on that day, he was standing in front of Pharaoh. God never writes a wasted word, and he does not keep wasted days either. The stretch of your life that looks most like a blank page may be exactly the stretch he is using to line things up.
Four kinds of heart, one season of waiting. And the one who waits it out beside us once waited three days in a tomb himself.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, towards God. Take that stretch of days you feel went for nothing, name it, bring it to God, and ask him to define it afresh: "Lord, those three years, those five years — what were you lining them up with?"
Second, towards yourself. Take the sentence inside you that says, "God has probably forgotten me," and change it into, "The time is not yet full." Write it down, and read it once every morning.

Third, towards people. Ask one person, "Are you all right today?" — and then listen to the whole of the answer, without interrupting and without hurrying to hand over a solution. The way Joseph did that morning.
Fourth, towards your daily living. Say one true and unpleasant thing this week, and say it carrying love. Pray before you say it, and look the other person in the eye while you say it.
Fifth, towards your calling. Right where you are standing now, serve somebody whose situation is harder than yours. If you are in a prison, then serve the people in the same prison.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. One: there is a man in the Bible who did somebody a very large favour, and the moment that person turned away he forgot him — forgot him for two whole years. Two: only two years later did it become clear that if he had got out early what he would have got was his freedom, and because he got out late what he got was an entire country. Three: so I have learned one thing — people forget, and God does not.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will not stake my hope on any person's memory; the one who remembers me has not forgotten.
I declare that even in my own hard season I will still see the faces of the people around me.
I declare that in the places where nobody can see me, there too I will give God the glory.
I declare that my days of waiting are not a blank page; God is lining up his own timing.
"Give God the glory in the small places" this week — will that not come across as an affectation?

Whether it sounds affected depends on whether what you are saying is true. Here are three very natural ways to do it. First, put "thank you for the kind word" together with the facts: "God really did help with this one; at the start I could not get hold of the direction at all." You do not need to add a long string of spiritual vocabulary. Second, say out loud what other people contributed: giving God the glory does not mean erasing your co-workers, and being clear about who helped you is itself a form of honesty. Third, do it privately first: give thanks once when it is only you and God, and then the sentence you say in public will not come out hollow. Do it long enough and it stops being an affectation, because by then it is genuinely what you think.
This chapter ends on a very cold sentence: "Yet the chief cup bearer didn't remember Joseph, but forgot him."

If the Bible stopped writing there, this would simply be the story of a good man who got nothing for it. But the Bible does not stop writing there. Turn one page and the first line is "At the end of two full years" — that is not a full stop. It is the mark of a stretch of time being brought into alignment.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because if my hope rests on the cup bearer, I will hate him for two years; and if my hope rests on the God who remembers me, then I can go on inside the prison asking people, "Are you all right today?" And at Golgotha there was a man who asked one thing only, "remember me" — and the one beside him said, there and then: today you will be with me in Paradise.

May God bless every one of us: that in the days of being forgotten we would not grow bitter, and in the days of waiting we would not stop serving; and may we remember that our names are not written in anybody's memory — they are engraved on the palms of his hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson home as a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ He was in prison himself, and yet he saw the look on somebody else's face. Why is still being able to see people while you are in pain a sign of spiritual health?
2. ★★ "Don't interpretations belong to God?" — what makes it hard to hand God the only piece of leverage you have left?
3. ★ He knew how ugly the answer was and he still told it straight. How does the truth have to be told for it to be pastoral care and not merely correct?
4. ★★ Asking a person for help is not unbelief. How do those two things hold together at once — putting your hope in God, and putting your request into human ears?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone speaks in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I do not have to ask anybody), fearful (I am afraid of being passed over one more time), ashamed (I am the one nobody remembers), wounded (the person I helped turned away and forgot me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read this aloud: "Why do you look so sad today?" Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something inside you that you waited a long time for and that never came to anything? What has that thing turned you into by now?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The person I most want to be remembered by is …"
9. ★★ This week, which one person are you going to ask, "Are you all right today?" — and then listen to the whole answer? Say the name.

Leader's reminder: the question about a long wait that never came to anything will touch on years of waiting and on the hurt of being let down. Do not round it off quickly with "God has a good purpose in it"; let the person finish first. If someone has already come as far as bitterness or exhaustion, stay with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, whose face is the one you most often fail to see? How will you make that up this week?

11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your area of service, who is the forgotten benefactor — the one who did the favour and never got remembered, the way the cup bearer never remembered Joseph?
12. ★★★ The practice of giving glory: this week, when you are praised, let your first sentence name God and your co-workers. Say now what it is you are likely to be praised for shortly.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and this week ask each other every day, "Are you all right today?" Say his name here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who was locked up on a charge he never earned, and one morning he saw that two new prisoners looked unhappy and went over of his own accord to ask them what was wrong. Second: he helped one of them, and asked only that the man remember him once he was out — and the man forgot him for two years. Third: so what I learned is that people forget, but the person you become while you wait is never wasted. Write down here and now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the thing you waited a long time for that never came to anything, and the person you are going to go and ask after this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that in the days of being forgotten we would still be able to see other people's faces.
